summary: This document defines how to use the ARIA block cipher in the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol. It covers two modes, counter mode and Galois/Counter mode, the key derivation, and the profiles needed for DTLS-SRTP and MIKEY.

plainLanguage.summary: ARIA is a scrambling method. This explains how to use it to protect audio and video calls so only the people on the call can understand them.

subtitle: Secure real-time media using the ARIA block cipher.

tldr.problem: Applications need to securely encrypt audio and video streams in real time. The ARIA block cipher is a proven encryption standard, but no one had specified how to use it within SRTP's framework.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8269 defines two encryption modes (Counter and GCM) for ARIA, describes how to derive keys within SRTP, and registers protection profiles so implementations can negotiate ARIA-based encryption for voice and video calls.
tldr.outcome: Systems can now encrypt RTP streams using ARIA instead of just AES, giving deployments in regions where ARIA is preferred a standard way to protect real-time media.

today: RFC 8269 is an Informational RFC published in October 2017. It has not been obsoleted and provides the standard definition for using ARIA within SRTP. The six protection profiles are registered with IANA and available for implementation.

sections.title: Introduction to ARIA
sections.content:
ARIA is a block cipher algorithm, a method for scrambling data invented by Korean cryptographers in 2003. It encrypts 128-bit blocks of data using keys of 128, 192, or 256 bits, completing the scrambling in 12, 14, or 16 rounds depending on the key size. The algorithm is secure, efficient on both powerful computers and tiny 8-bit processors, and has been a Korean industry standard since 2004. It is widely used in government services there and was added to international cryptography standards in 2007.

This RFC shows how to use ARIA in the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP), which protects live media such as voice and video calls over the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: ARIA is a scrambler that was invented in Korea and works well on all kinds of computers. This RFC says how to use it to protect phone calls.

sections.title: Two Encryption Modes
sections.content:
ARIA works with SRTP using two proven encryption modes. The first is Counter Mode (ARIA-CTR), which processes the plaintext stream by encrypting a stream of counter values and combining them with the data. This approach requires a separate authentication algorithm such as HMAC-SHA1 to prove the message has not been altered. The second is Galois/Counter Mode (ARIA-GCM), which combines encryption and authentication in one operation, so a receiving system can both decrypt and verify the message in a single step, making it more efficient.

Both modes work exactly like the equivalent AES modes already used in SRTP, so existing SRTP implementations can swap in ARIA by replacing the AES cipher while keeping everything else the same.
sections.plainLanguage: ARIA uses the same scrambling tricks as the cipher everyone already uses, so engineers can switch to ARIA without learning a whole new method.

sections.title: Key Derivation
sections.content: Before using ARIA to encrypt media, the SRTP system must derive encryption and authentication keys from a master key. This derivation function is called ARIA-CTR PRF (Pseudorandom Function). The PRF follows the same procedure as the AES key derivation function already defined in SRTP: it uses ARIA in Counter Mode to generate the stream of key material, with different salt values for the encryption key, authentication key, and other purposes. ARIA-128 systems use 128-bit keys and ARIA-256 systems use 256-bit keys; the RFC defines the PRF for both.
sections.plainLanguage: Just like with AES, you start with a secret and run it through ARIA to make the actual keys used for protecting each call.

sections.title: Protection Profiles
sections.content:
The RFC registers six protection profiles. Four use ARIA-CTR with HMAC-SHA1 authentication: two use 128-bit ARIA keys and produce 80-bit or 32-bit authentication tags, and two use 256-bit keys with the same tag sizes. The other two use ARIA-GCM with 128-bit or 256-bit keys, producing 128-bit authentication tags as part of the GCM mode. Each profile is identified by a numeric code registered with IANA so that DTLS (the protocol used to negotiate encryption for SRTP) can unambiguously refer to it. The RFC also defines how these profiles map to parameters in MIKEY, the Multimedia Internet KEYing protocol used when key agreement must happen outside of DTLS.

The profiles with 32-bit authentication tags are allowed for applications where smaller tags are acceptable, though 80-bit tags are recommended for general use.
sections.plainLanguage: These are official combinations of ARIA with different key sizes and authentication methods. Phones and videoconference systems pick one based on what they need.

sections.title: Security and Status
sections.content:
At the time of publication, no practical attacks on ARIA were known. The document notes that SRTP traditionally used HMAC-SHA1 as the standard authentication algorithm, but due to theoretical concerns about SHA-1, the IETF has been moving toward stronger hash functions like SHA-2. However, HMAC-SHA1 is secure enough for authentication when used as part of SRTP, even if SHA-1 itself should be avoided for digital signatures. Implementations MAY use shorter authentication tags where the application allows, but SHOULD prefer 80-bit tags for general use.

This is an Informational RFC, meaning it documents a protocol detail without standardizing it as a requirement, but IANA has registered the profiles for deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: ARIA itself has no known weaknesses. The older SHA-1 hash is a bit old, but it's still safe when used this way. This RFC lets people use ARIA if they want to.
